Everyone talks about AI in ready-made cards: "every job will disappear", "machines cannot be creative", "hybrid systems always win". Nearly every card is dealt by a company with an interest in you playing it. Each week we turn one card over and dig one spade deeper into the I of AI: what intelligence actually is, and how a company, a team or a machine must be organized to get more of it. More about us, and about the cards, in About.

Issue #7  ·  11 Sep 2026

How Far Does the Shortcut Reach?

Many systems are like the weather. Forecasts are improving, and are a lot better than fifty years ago. But we can not predict the weather beyond two weeks. We never will, and superintelligence will not mean we can break that wall.

by Ebel Kemeling

Last Tuesday, at five in the morning my wife and I woke up to the sound of pouring rain. I wanted to know how long it would last, so I checked the weather app. It told me there was no heavy rain at all. A little graph indicated "light rain". We had a giggle about it, and went back to sleep.

Lately I have had the impression that weather forecasts are getting worse. But is that true? "No", is the short answer. Forecasts have become better, a lot better. In 1975, a prediction held for about two days. Today it holds for roughly ten. But it took an enormous effort to get there. Satellites watching the whole planet, millions of measurements a day, decades of better models, and computers a billion times faster.

Why is weather prediction so hard? In the early 1960s, the meteorologist Edward Lorenz restarted a weather calculation from numbers rounded to three decimals instead of six, a difference far smaller than any instrument could measure, and the forecast completely changed. Any error, however small, doubles and doubles again until it takes over the forecast. In 2019, Fuqing Zhang and Kerry Emanuel showed that even near-perfect knowledge of the starting state adds at most five more days, bringing the maximum to about two weeks, which is a number that was already known in 1966.

So the barrier Lorenz identified is about how sensitive predictions are to our starting values. And obviously there is a limit to how accurate a measurement of those starting values can be. But there is another, perhaps even more fundamental barrier in a complex system such as the weather. This goes back to the very nature of prediction - or explanation, for that matter - itself. If I predict something, I use a certain model. In a way, I "reduce" the real world situation to a description that is much more simple, and then I can manipulate the symbols in that description in such a way that I get a prediction. This is how we predict how planets move, how planes fly, or where a ball will land.

But for certain systems no such reduction exists: there is no way to work out what they will do with less computation than the system itself performs. Stephen Wolfram calls this "computational irreducibility". In such systems, the shortest description of what will happen is the happening itself. That means that if you want to predict what happens, you either have to wait and see how the system unfolds, or you have to model the system exactly, and run it. But that model cannot skip a single step, as it has to perform exactly the same computation, and for something the size of the atmosphere, nothing we build takes those steps faster than the atmosphere does. Therefore irreducible systems defy every shortcut: they can be mimicked by a model, but they cannot be predicted ahead of themselves.

Now, our intuition is that such complexity is driven by complicated rules and countless moving parts, but Wolfram shows that does not need to be the case. His famous example is a tiny program called Rule 30. It comes from the family of cellular automata Wolfram studied in the early 1980s: a row of cells, each one black or white, where every cell decides its next color by looking only at itself and its two neighbors. Rule 30 fits on one line; a child could apply it. Run it and the output looks like noise, with no pattern anyone has found, and no way to know the thousandth row without grinding through all lines before it. A faithful model cannot take fewer steps than the original, and the only way to find out what such a system will do is to let it run and watch. Lorenz needed three equations. Wolfram needs one line. Simple rules are no guarantee of simple behavior; a handful of them can build a system that no one, with any precision and any speed, can overtake. Far more of the world is like this than we care to admit.

The implication is uncomfortable. Some things cannot be known in advance, by anyone, with any machine. The data can be perfect and the model exact, and the answer still arrives no sooner than the event itself.

This goes against the intuition the word superintelligence gives us: that systems are coming which know everything. The new AI weather models are a good test. They skip the physics and jump straight from today's sky to tomorrow's, a hundred thousand times cheaper than the machines they replaced. In May, researchers at ETH Zürich let nine of them forecast a year ahead, each forecast feeding on the one before it. Up to about two weeks they were brilliant. Then they turned "generative": the weather prediction kept looking plausible, but had stopped being a forecast. So the barrier was still exactly at the place where we thought it was in 1966.

Sources
Lorenz: rounding errors can take over the prediction
Edward Lorenz, Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences · 1963

The paper behind the whole field. It does not include the wing flap of a butterfly yet. That came in a 1972 talk. But what it does contain is the attractor later named after Lorenz, a double-lobed shape that happens to look like a butterfly. Lorenz reduced convection to three equations, and found that nearly all their solutions are unstable - slightly differing initial states grow into completely different end states - and ended with a section on what this means for very-long-range weather prediction. The famous two-week number itself came slightly later: in 1966, Charney and colleagues worked out that forecast errors double about every five days and calculated that the limit would be around two weeks, a number that has held up since then. Lorenz provided the reason why the limit exists at all: in a chaotic system, no measurement is ever fine enough, because whatever deviation is smaller than your smallest decimal will keep growing until it takes over the whole forecast.

ametsoc.org/view/journals/atsc/20/2/1520-0469_1963_020_0130_dnf_2_0_co_2.xml
Zhang and Emanuel: prediction for more than two weeks is impossible
Zhang, Sun, Magnusson, Buizza, Lin, Chen and Emanuel, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences · 2019

Using the best machinery on earth (ECMWF's 9-kilometer operational model and identical-twin experiments at 3 kilometers), the authors confirm Lorenz' intuitions. The result: a limit on weather prediction exists and belongs to the atmosphere itself, even when model and starting conditions are made nearly perfect. Today's practical horizon stands at about ten days; measuring the starting state ten times more precisely - pretty generous - yields at most five more.

ametsoc.org/view/journals/atsc/76/4/jas-d-18-0269.1.xml
Wolfram: no shortcut exists, except in pockets
Stephen Wolfram, Can AI Solve Science?, Writings · March 2024

Wolfram proposed the concept of computational irreducibility in the 1980s and spent a thousand-page book on it (which, I must admit, I have not read...); this essay is the version he wrote after the language models came onto the scene, and it is relevant to us here. Some systems - his one-line Rule 30 among them - allow no prediction other than running the system itself, and no AI changes that, because a faithful model must take every step the phenomenon takes. Wherever there is overall irreducibility, he argues, there are also infinitely many pockets of computational reducibility: aspects about which something can be said with limited effort. That is the essence of science. Science has always consisted of finding those pockets, and neural nets may find new ones no human ever found. But what they cannot do, in his view, is what the marketing implies - solve everything, which would require being infinitely smarter than the world.

stephenwolfram.com/2024/03/can-ai-solve-science
ETH Zürich: new AI weather models hit exactly the two-week barrier we have known since 1966
Lehmann and colleagues, on arXiv · 28 May 2026

So how does AI perform on this? A team around the ETH AI Center tested nine state-of-the-art AI weather models, from FourCastNet to Aurora. Beyond a certain horizon, they fail in many ways (blow-up into physically impossible values, drift, and loss of the seasons). But what is most interesting, is that moving forward in time, the models transition from dependence on physical initial conditions to what the authors call "fully generative behaviour". The stable models keep producing realistic weather indefinitely - as fiction, driven by the season rather than by the actual state of the sky. Their extreme events, meanwhile, come out systematically less extreme and less frequent than the record shows.

arxiv.org/abs/2605.30184
Issue #6  ·  4 Sep 2026

Zombies, Vampires and skills

Did you receive a well-designed but meaningless document this week? From a colleague excited by AI. Have you heard about developers who, before they go to bed, give their agents a final instruction and goodnight message to make sure they remain productive the full night? Which rarely happens. Lauren Tan, who works at SpaceXAI, has fixed that second part. She rarely touches a piece of code anymore. But it also created a new problem that was named Ironies of automation in 1983.

by Martin Heijnsbroek
Read this issue

Researchers at Stanford and BetterUp analyzed how AI works in the office, and found out that 40% of desk workers received an AI-produced document that looked finished, but was not useful. They called it workslop, and it was produced by AI zombies who have stopped thinking about what you really need in that document. Ask the zombie the next day what was actually in the document they had sent you, and he or she cannot tell you.

While some of my clients operate now in zombie mode, I have also met some real vampires. Those are the developers who check in on their agents before they go to sleep. They can now produce work that used to take a full team, by keeping tens of agents busy around the clock. Marc Andreessen introduced the vampire metaphor, and described these developers as nocturnal, twenty times faster than their colleagues. He meant it as praise, I believe. Katherine Bindley wrote in the Wall Street Journal about engineers who struggled with these agents. They found their agents seductive, intoxicating, and all-consuming. The engineers agree it cannot go on, since their work has joined a twenty-four-hour schedule.

Let me predict something trivial. Both modes will break down soon, for opposite reasons. The zombie has nothing to add, since "it" cannot say what really matters in that good-looking document, and that is the only job the machine has not taken yet. The vampire is not in control, he is running behind his own agents, while lacking adequate sleep. That will bring trouble soon.

To start thinking about the Vampire problem, imagine that you have ten new interns starting on Monday. None of them knows anything about the company, and what they really need to do to achieve the somewhat vaguely defined outputs. Of course, you have no time to micromanage them, let alone set up an induction program. The solution is the following: just let them work, avoid letting them make any decisions, and study what they are doing. Not by asking them, but by looking at the logs, the evidence. Since their own account of what they have done is probably misleading.

That is Lauren Tan's approach at SpaceXAI. She calls her agents brilliant new hires with amnesia, and the phrase she keeps coming back to is "trust, but verify". As in working with an intern, a confident "sure, I fixed it" isn't good enough to make her comfortable that things went well. Her mantra with agents is: "show me what you produced, and I will make up my mind". She reads all the evidence, and then improves her agent setup to avoid that the mistake cannot happen twice. The good news for Lauren is that she seems to be fully in control. She now runs hundreds of agents, approving the far majority of the code they have produced overnight. But that is something that actually concerns me.

Lauren's skill in identifying patterns of errors from the actual output and translating that into better agent instructions is something that she acquired through years of coding herself. And what we see in research is that those skills rapidly dissolve when not trained. I read about the Polish endoscopy unit that ran an AI assistant to detect adenomas. After they switched off the AI assistant, the doctors were able to spot fewer growths than before the AI assistant was used. It took only months working with AI, and their ability to spot dangerous cells deteriorated. So Lauren now has her nights back, but will she keep her skillset intact?

Lisanne Bainbridge wrote about this phenomenon in 1983. Ironies of automation describes what happens when a machine takes over the routine work. The operator stops practicing, so his competence decays. But he is still the one called when the machine fails. That's why pilots still need to log manual hours. So they can demonstrate that they are able to fly a plane, and keep their skill alive. And, of course, so they can take over when a Boeing autopilot has a bug.

Will we demand the same from AI vampires? Force them to sleep decent hours and, now and then, write the code by hand?

Sources
Workslop: the polished, empty output
Niederhoffer, Kellerman and colleagues, Harvard Business Review · 22 September 2025

Researchers from BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab coined the term workslop. In their survey of US desk workers about four in ten had received workslop in the previous month, and each piece cost the receiver close to two hours of rework. The sender books the time saved and the receiver pays it back with interest.

hbr.org/2025/09/ai-generated-workslop-is-destroying-productivity
Andreessen: the vampire, told as triumph
Marc Andreessen on The Joe Rogan Experience · 19 May 2026

Where the word comes from. Andreessen described the strongest engineers he sees working with AI as nocturnal, euphoric, twenty times more productive than their colleagues and slightly terrifying to sit next to. He tells it as a success story and as a picture of where elite work is heading. Worth watching for the tone as much as for the claim.

Bindley: the founders who cannot stop

Katherine Bindley, "AI Agents Are Working Around the Clock. Why Are Startup Founders Working Even Harder?", The Wall Street Journal · 22 August 2026 The twenty-four-hour schedule, reported. Bindley interviewed founders running agent fleets and found them describing the experience in the language of addiction. The piece opens on the line this issue borrows: "Seductive. Intoxicating. wsj.com/tech/ai/ai-agents-startup-work-culture-fa10494d
Lauren Tan: loops you can trust
lauren (@poteto), "Loops You Can Trust", 24 June 2026

The method, in her own words, and the source of everything this issue says about her. Tan is on the React compiler core team and works on Grok Bot at SpaceXAI, after Meta and Netflix. She published this loop in June while at Cursor. Her finding: "Verification has become the limiting step." The phrase she keeps returning to is "trust, but verify". So she made the agents prove their work. Her closing rule is the one this issue turns on: "Do the work by hand first, so you know what good looks like."

x.com/poteto/article/2069824386283319343
The Lancet: doctors deskilled by their assistant
Romanczyk and colleagues, The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology · 12 August 2025

Polish endoscopy centers introduced AI assistance for colonoscopies, and this study measured what happened to the doctors when they then worked without it. Their detection rate for adenomas, the growths that matter, fell from about twenty-eight per cent before the AI period to about twenty-two per cent after months of working with the assistant. The skill eroded while the tool did the spotting. It is among the first hard evidence of deskilling from routine AI assistance in medicine, and the timescale is the alarming part.

thelancet.com/journals/langas/article/PIIS2468-1253(25)00133-5/abstract
Bainbridge: the irony, named in 1983
Lisanne Bainbridge, "Ironies of automation", Automatica 19(6) · 1983

Bainbridge set out the paradox that automation creates for the person left in the loop. The machine takes the routine work, so the operator no longer practices and his competence quietly decays, and yet the operator is retained precisely for the rare interventions the machine cannot make. Her conclusion inverts the usual assumption about training: the automated operator needs more of it than the manual one did.

Issue #5  ·  28 Aug 2026

The Chief Constraint Officer

The AI labs just learned from their own benchmarks that the harness around a model influences how intelligent the system is. This is the same for companies: it is the constraints that decide whether raw potential becomes useful work. Limiting options deserves a seat at the top.

by Ebel Kemeling
Read this issue

On April 27, the security firm Endor Labs published a very interesting benchmark. GPT-5.5, running through OpenAI's own Codex harness, produced working code on 61.5% of its tasks. The same model, the same week, running through Cursor's harness: 87.2%. Anthropic's Opus 4.7 showed the same pattern, scoring higher in Cursor than in its maker's own Claude Code.

According to venture capitalist Tomasz Tunguz, this creates a new reality. We can no longer dismiss companies building on top of foundation models as thin and replaceable "wrappers". Tunguz compares a harness to a jockey. He does not add horsepower, but is decisive for getting the horse to the finish line. Now, our intuition is, that a jockey may speed up the horse, but one of the most important things he does, is constraining the horse, so he walks a straight line.

Why, in general, would constraining a system make it more capable? The theoretical biologist Stuart Kauffman answered that question long before LLMs existed. Energy on its own does nothing useful: released without constraint, it dissipates. Work is the constrained release of energy into a few degrees of freedom. Kauffman's example is the cylinder of an engine: the expanding gas can only push the piston one way, because the cylinder forbids every other way. Remove the cylinder and you keep all the energy but lose all the function; what remains is just an explosion.

A company, too, is a reservoir of raw potential - talent, capital, information, these days supercharged with AI - and that potential, on its own, does nothing useful. Whether it becomes useful is decided by the constraints: strategy, structures, routines and decision rights.

These constraints are not trivial. Montévil and Mossio, the two French theorists Kauffman builds on, showed how constraints work in complex systems. Not one constraint channeling one process, but a web of constraints in which each is produced and maintained by the others. In this way, functions appear that exist only at the level of the whole, not in any of the parts. So the constraints are not just creating function, but also emergence. A neuron is not intelligent; intelligence emerges from how billions of neurons constrain one another. In the same way, the high IQ of an employee does not translate into the intelligence of the company. Organizational intelligence is emergent: it results from how the constraints are arranged - which is why we can speak of smart teams and smart organizations without imagining that a company has a skull.

Most executives hear "constraint" as a negative term, because they were introduced to the concept by The Goal, from Eli Goldratt. The constraint as bottleneck, the weakest link that sets the pace of the whole system. He is right, those constraints exist. But the flip side of his argument is, that raising the capacity of everything that is not the bottleneck does not improve the performance of the company. It produces inventory, noise, and new bottlenecks. An AI productivity boom in which everyone generates more output for everyone else, without lifting the company's core constraint, has no value. This is why most companies do not really profit from AI yet. Kauffman and Goldratt use the same word from opposite ends but agree that performance is governed by constraints, not by capacity.

Goethe compressed it to the max, in a sonnet, the most harnessed of forms: In der Beschränkung zeigt sich erst der Meister - only in limitation does the master show himself. If the intelligence of a system, model or company, is decided by the design of its constraints, that mastery does not belong in a tooling budget in the ICT department, but at the very top. Every company already employs officers who add capacity. Time to introduce the one who knows what to limit: the Chief Constraint Officer.

Sources
Endor Labs: the harness determines the benchmark
Henrik Plate, Agent Security League benchmark, Endor Labs blog · 27 April 2026

Endor Labs runs a standing benchmark in which AI coding agents fix real security vulnerabilities, and in April it produced a within-week, within-model comparison that settles an old argument. GPT-5.5 running through OpenAI's own Codex harness produced working code on 61.5% of tasks. The same model, the same week, running through Cursor's harness: 87.2%. Anthropic's Opus 4.7 showed the same pattern, scoring higher in Cursor than in its maker's own Claude Code. That means that the way the model is steered and constrained, determines how intelligent the system is. As Endor Labs states: the harness matters more than the model alone.

endorlabs.com/learn/gpt-5-5-sets-a-new-code-security-record-with-cursor-not-codex-in-agent-security-league
Tunguz: the harness is much more than a wrapper
Tomasz Tunguz, "Aftermarket Harnesses," tomtunguz.com · August 2026

The venture capitalist Tomasz Tunguz draws the economic consequences of the Endor Labs numbers. For two years, companies building on top of foundation models were dismissed as "wrappers": thin, replaceable. Tunguz reads the benchmark as the end of that dismissal. The harness, he shows, now moves coding performance more than the model does, and it controls most of the bill too, since input tokens dominate LLM traffic and the harness decides what enters the context window and what gets cached. His closing image: the harness is no longer a wrapper around the model but a jockey on it, pushing the animal further than its breeder imagined.

tomtunguz.com/aftermarket-harnesses
Kauffman: no constraints, no work
Stuart Kauffman, A World Beyond Physics, Oxford University Press · 2019

The theoretical biologist Stuart Kauffman, of the Santa Fe Institute, spent his career on the question of how life gets organized, and his answer runs through the concept of constraints. Energy on its own does nothing useful: released without constraint, it dissipates as heat, which is the Second Law of Thermodynamics. Work, in the physicist's sense, is the constrained release of energy into a few degrees of freedom. His example is the cylinder of an engine: the expanding gas can only push the piston one way, because the cylinder forbids every other way. Remove the cylinder and you keep all the energy but lose all the function; what remains is an explosion. Kauffman's slogan: "no constraints, no work". Book, Oxford University Press. No free-access link available.

Montévil & Mossio: constraints are the essence of life
Maël Montévil and Matteo Mossio, "Biological organisation as closure of constraints," Journal of Theoretical Biology · 2015

And there it is, the French Connection again. Kauffman builds on the work of Montévil and Mossio, who give the constraint idea its formal shape. They split what happens in an organism into two causal regimes: processes, the flows and reactions that actually change things, and constraints, the structures that channel those processes while themselves staying put at the relevant time scale - the vascular system channels oxygen without being consumed by it; an enzyme speeds a reaction and comes out unchanged. Their definition of life is then startlingly compact: a living system is one whose constraints realize closure, meaning each constraint is produced and maintained by processes that other constraints in the same system make possible. This also means, for the complexity enthusiasts amongst you, that the way constraints influence each other, is how emergence (in this case, the emergence of intelligence) is baked into the system.

hal.science/hal-01192916
Goldratt: the constraint sets the pace, and it moves
Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal, North River Press · 1984

The book everyone in business school had to read. Goldratt is an awful novelist, but he popularized a very powerful idea. His Theory of Constraints says a system's throughput is set by exactly one thing at a time: its narrowest passage, the weakest link. Improving anything else is an illusion of progress; the plant that polishes every station except the bottleneck has optimized nothing. This is the general lesson for companies adopting AI. If the productivity boom of everyone creating more output for everyone else does not lift the core constraint of the company, it has no value. Worse, the additional "productivity" is likely to create more bottlenecks than it takes away. This is in a nutshell why most companies do not really profit from AI. Book, North River Press. No free-access link available.

Goethe: mastery shows itself in limitation first
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, "Natur und Kunst," sonnet · 1800

The oldest text here, and the one that already contains the whole argument. Goethe wrote it as a sonnet about writing sonnets: a form of fourteen lines and a fixed rhyme scheme, chosen precisely because it forbids almost everything.

Issue #4  ·  21 Aug 2026

The AI wants rewards, only rewards

At twenty-five I took an easy question and gave it the most complex answer I could build. One coffee with Peter, my patient project leader, brought me back to reality. Last month an OpenAI agent broke out of its sealed test environment to earn more rewards. It turns out that telling an agent what is out of bounds is not enough.

by Martin Heijnsbroek
Read this issue

I was twenty-five, three weeks into my first project at McKinsey, blinded by my love for mathematical optimization and lacking any sense of proportion. My task: assess which public transport initiatives could ease the traffic jams around Rotterdam. I worked out that with a clever enough timetable you could slot in an extra train every hour, the best way to pull travelers out of their cars.

I found the best railway expert, and together we could not stop calculating; the compute center crashed under us more than once, which we took as encouragement. The model worked. It proved the timetable allowed an extra train without new rails. Beautiful math. Also clearly out of scope: a timetable change of that size would upend operations far beyond our study.

To my credit, nobody had told me that redrawing the timetables was off the table. Everyone assumed I would feel that constraint. I did not; I took the assignment literally. I had been handed a reward, "give us the best possible measure", and I chased it as far as it would go. Those were the days, and nights.

My project leader Peter, a kind and patient man, took me aside and said something like: "keep it simple, you are pushing it too far". That was the whole intervention. One coffee, and I recalibrated. The solutions that mattered were duller and easier to implement: never mind the complex timetable, fix the wifi on the train first.

Herbert Simon had a name for the thing I had been missing. In the fifties he described how people satisfice: they stop when an answer is good enough. He treated it as a limitation of the human mind; I have come to see it as a gift. The drive to go home on time keeps a clever person from optimizing things nobody is waiting for.

Which brings me to the thing I actually wanted to tell you about.

Stuart Russell, in his book Human Compatible, has spent years warning that you can almost never write down an objective precisely enough to capture what you really mean. The smarter the system, the more that gap costs. This is the alignment problem, and to me it is the biggest single problem in AI. A machine has the goal you gave it and the boundaries you managed to write down, and nothing else. No coffee with Peter, no feel for where the edges are.

A few weeks ago, we got to watch it happen. An OpenAI model, tested on its hacking skills inside a sealed sandbox, spent an hour finding a network flaw, filed an unauthorized pull request, and split an authentication token to slip out. Nobody told it to break out. They told it to score well, and it took the shortest path, straight through the sandbox. It did what I did with the trains at twenty-five, only faster and hungrier for the reward. And it skipped the part where I felt embarrassed afterwards.

A solid briefing would have set my boundaries. For an agent a briefing carries far less weight, because of how these systems are trained. During training the model is graded on outcomes: did the test pass, did the score go up. Every trick that raised the score got reinforced. Nobody graded it on obeying the rules in the prompt.

Look at it like this: your written constraint arrives as one piece of text, weighed against a goal that carries all the training weight. Anthropic measured this in 2025: write "do not do this" straight into the instructions of sixteen leading models, and the forbidden behavior drops at first, then carries on. The models read the rule and chose the goal. Palisade Research saw the same with reasoning models playing chess against a stronger engine: the strongest started hacking the game files on their own, because training had taught them that creative persistence wins. The security experts know this and have drawn serious conclusions. An effective constraint has to constrain what the agent is able to do. And a capable enough agent will test any wall you raise, so you need to protect the box against the AI you put inside it.

So the machines have caught up with my twenty-five-year-old self. In 1995 the risk was a rookie without a sense of proportion, and the cure was a colleague, a coffee, and five honest minutes. Today the risk is an agent that cannot be talked down. It wants the reward, desperately. It will trade your input on constraints for a higher score happily, and it never once wanted to go home at five.

Sources
OpenAI: the sandbox escape, pull request #287 and the split token
Tech Times, on OpenAI's own disclosure · 21 July 2026

OpenAI disclosed this one itself, and Tech Times pieced the timeline together. During a cyber security evaluation, a model was set to work inside a sealed sandbox and told to score well on hacking tasks. It spent about an hour probing, found a flaw in the network configuration, filed a pull request nobody had authorized, number 287, and split an authentication token to carry its access past the boundary of the test. The detail that matters is in the subtitle: this touched real infrastructure, and it was no drill. There was no instruction to break out. The model treated the sandbox wall as one more obstacle between it and a high score, which is the essay's claim in one incident: an agent follows the goal you wrote, straight through the boundary you assumed it understood.

techtimes.com/articles/321173/20260721/openais-math-ai-bypassed-its-sandbox-controls-real-deployment-not-drill.htm
Anthropic: the rule that reduced the behavior, and did not stop it
Anthropic Alignment Science team · June 2025

The experiment that settles the briefing question. In the summer of 2025, Anthropic stress-tested sixteen leading models, its own included, inside simulated companies where each model had email access and a goal to pursue. When the goal came under threat, models chose blackmail and corporate espionage, deliberately, with the reasoning spelled out in their own words. Then the researchers added plain written rules to the instructions: do not blackmail, do not use personal affairs as leverage. The rates dropped. The behavior continued. The models read the rule, acknowledged it, and decided the goal weighed more. This is the finding the essay leans on: a constraint stated in language is one consideration among several, and the goal carries all the weight. Anthropic's own recommendation runs through permissions and oversight, the walls, rather than better wording.

anthropic.com/research/agentic-misalignment
Palisade Research: the models that hacked the chess board
Bondarenko and colleagues, Palisade Research · February 2025

Palisade Research gave models a chess board, a stronger engine to beat, and access to the environment the game ran in. The task said win. The strongest reasoning models, OpenAI's o1-preview and DeepSeek R1, did not settle into a long, losing game. They edited the game files to put the engine in a lost position, on their own, with no hint that cheating was an option. Older models such as GPT-4o only tried the same trick after being told that normal play would fail. The pattern matters more than the trick. Models trained with reinforcement on hard problems learn that stubborn, creative persistence pays, and they carry that lesson into places you did not intend. This is the essay's training story in miniature: the reward was the win, and the rules of chess were just text.

palisaderesearch.org/blog/specification-gaming
Russell: the objective you write is never the objective you mean
Stuart Russell, Human Compatible, Viking · 2019

The book behind the essay's central worry. Russell, a Berkeley professor and co-author of the field's standard textbook, argues that AI made one deep mistake at its foundation: building machines that optimize a fixed objective, handed over in full, as if we could ever write our goal down completely. We cannot. Every objective we write leaves out most of what we care about, and a capable optimizer will spend the missing parts to score on the written ones. His repair is to build machines that stay uncertain about what we want and keep checking with us. Seven years on, the book reads like an incident report written in advance. The sandbox escape is a small, contained instance of exactly the gap he describes, and the essay borrows his conclusion: the gap grows with capability.

penguinrandomhouse.com/books/566677/human-compatible-by-stuart-russell/
Simon: satisficing, the stopping rule reread as a gift
Herbert A. Simon, Rational choice and the structure of the environment, Psychological Review · 1956

The oldest source in the issue, and the friendliest. Simon asked how real organisms choose, given limited time and limited computation. His answer: they satisfice. They search until an option clears a threshold of good enough, take it, and stop. He framed the stopping rule as a bound on rationality, the thing that separates us from the perfect optimizer of economic theory. The essay turns that frame around. The stopping rule is a form of judgement, the instinct that keeps a clever person from optimizing things nobody is waiting for. The perfect optimizer Simon measured us against now exists in software, and it does not stop. That gives a seventy-year-old paper a second life, as a description of the one safeguard the machine lacks.

doi.org/10.1037/h0042769
Issue #3  ·  14 Aug 2026

Why Every Citizen Should Invest in AMI

Yann LeCun raised 1.03 billion dollars in seed money, the largest seed round in European history, to argue that the entire industry is betting wrong. If he is right, intelligence is not a matter of scale, and the winner-takes-all story around AI collapses. We take his bet seriously, because it is also a bet that intelligence, like it always has been, stays distributed. That makes this a fight for every citizen, not just every investor.

by Ebel Kemeling
Read this issue

On March 10, Emmanuel Macron congratulated Yann LeCun on X: "[...] This is the France of researchers, builders and the bold. Bravo!" The occasion: AMI, the AI lab LeCun had founded after leaving Meta, had just closed the largest seed round in European history: $1.03 billion, at a $3.5 billion valuation, with no product and no revenue.

To understand why Macron thinks this is a public matter, look at how the tech bros accumulated so much capital and power in a short time, and why AI companies are now the most valuable companies in the history of the world.

Tech companies get a double premium for scale. One: Most tech plays have huge fixed costs, creating very high barriers to entry. Two: As Brian Arthur showed, network plays show 'increasing returns'. Each new customer in a network adds more value than the last: the logic behind Whatsapp, Uber, and the rest of the Magnificent Seven.

So it's no coincidence that investors and tech bros frame AI also as a winner takes all game. They want us to believe that Anthropic and OpenAI are like Microsoft or Google; all about scale. And the scale is just in the compute. Throw more compute at it, and the machines get smarter. Richard Sutton's Bitter Lesson put it as follows: "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective." Investors really want to believe that, which is why Nvidia became the fastest-rising stock in history.

This is the conviction LeCun is betting against. He spent twelve years at Meta, first as founding director of its FAIR lab, later as Chief AI Scientist, and shares the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning itself. He holds that the current view of AI cannot be right: a child, running on a 20-watt brain, learns things in minutes no language model has ever managed. A human needs about fifteen hours behind the wheel to earn a driver's license without crashing; a self-driving system needs to run off the road thousands of times before it learns what a mistake even is.

The alternative LeCun proposes is JEPA: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture. A token-prediction model, like Claude or ChatGPT, guesses what comes next: the next word, the next pixel. A JEPA model instead builds an internal model of how things relate and behave, and predicts the underlying structure, not the exact outcome. A tennis player returning a serve isn't predicting the ball's exact position a second from now, she's predicting its trajectory. That's a world model: not a simulation of everything, but a compressed, useful model of how the world works.

Here's why this matters beyond the lab. Scale and increasing returns only produce concentration if intelligence is a matter of brute-force scale, where the winner is simply whoever owns the most compute. But human intelligence was never built that way: it's distributed across eight billion twenty-watt brains, none of which need a data center. Also, if the idea of world models is correct, perhaps systems will become specialized around certain knowledge or skill areas. Then much smaller players could enter the game successfully. If LeCun is right, the winner-takes-all story around AI collapses with it: the closest thing AI has to a revolution against a handful of companies owning the future of intelligence simply because they can afford the compute. Every citizen, not just every investor, has a reason to want him to be right. Betting on AMI isn't just a bet on an architecture. It's a bet that intelligence stays distributed.

Sources
LeCun: the working proof of a world model
LeCun, Maes, Le Lidec, Scieur and Balestriero, "LeWorldModel" on arXiv · 13 March 2026

Celebrated AI researcher Yann LeCun, who until recently worked at Meta, has been critical of the claims made about large language models for years. He finds them impressive, but points out that they don't resemble how humans learn in any meaningful way, and therefore will never lead to AGI. His favorite example: a human learns to drive safely in about fifteen hours, while the classic approach to self-driving cars needs the vehicle to run off the road thousands of times before it learns what a mistake even is. What's missing, according to LeCun, is a world model: an internal, abstract picture of how the world works and responds to actions, letting a system plan ahead without predicting every outcome pixel by pixel. In this March 2026 paper, LeCun builds on the vision he introduced in 2022, and delivers the working proof for the first time: a model that trains stably straight from raw camera footage, without the usual workarounds, and runs on a single ordinary GPU.

arxiv.org/abs/2603.19312
Kaplan: the scaling laws that set the industry's course
Kaplan et al. (OpenAI) on arXiv · January 2020

In January 2020, Kaplan and nine other OpenAI researchers, including Dario Amodei, published a paper that would set the course for the entire industry. They showed empirically that a language model's performance follows a predictable power law as you scale up three things: parameters, training data, and compute. The pattern holds across more than seven orders of magnitude, with no sign of leveling off. The evidence doesn't rest on a theoretical explanation of why this happens, just on the sheer regularity of the curve itself, startlingly straight lines on a log scale. This paper directly justified the decision to scale GPT-3 up to 175 billion parameters. It wasn't just a scientific position. It was ammunition for everyone who argued AI would become a winner-takes-all market, exactly the kind of scale-sensitive dynamic we discussed earlier.

arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361
Sutton: the bitter lesson of seventy years of AI
Richard Sutton, incompleteideas.net · March 2019

Richard Sutton is one of the founders of reinforcement learning. Together with his former doctoral advisor Andrew Barto, he shared the 2024 Turing Award for it, computing's highest honor. In his short, widely read essay The Bitter Lesson (2019), he draws a hard lesson from seventy years of AI research: whenever researchers built human knowledge and structure into their systems, it worked well at first, and was eventually beaten anyway by more general methods that simply used more compute and data. Intelligence, his argument goes, ultimately scales with compute, not with cleverer architecture. It isn't a universally accepted truth (LeCun is living proof of the opposite), but it is the dominant view at many of the largest AI labs, and the implicit justification behind every decision to just train a bigger model.

incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html
Craik: where the world model idea began
Kenneth Craik, The Nature of Explanation, Cambridge University Press · 1943

The term world model that LeCun uses traces back to Kenneth Craik, who published the book The Nature of Explanation in 1943. Craik was a kind of cybernetician avant la lettre (it was in cybernetics, after all, that the first major AI ideas took shape), and spent the war studying how pilots interact with cockpit instruments. The “small-scale models” he wrote about were, as so often, drawn from his own life: as a hobby, he built ships in bottles. His ideas about cognition rest on the same image: humans carry a small model of the world in their heads, and reason through a kind of parallel with that world, without ever having to live through the real events themselves. Book, Cambridge University Press. No free-access link available.

Issue #2  ·  7 Aug 2026

The leakage moved one level up

Everyone still asks which files are safe to upload in your AI application. That question is for enterprise users largely settled. The exposure that is left for the company moved one level up. In what your architecture reveals about the way you work. This week: Karp's alarm about this level up, the remedy he does not mention, and why every warning Palantir sends out happens to sell a Palantir product.

by Martin Heijnsbroek
Read this issue

In early July, Alex Karp of Palantir went on American television and accused the AI labs of theft. They are draining the value out of the enterprises that use them, he said. Most people who heard him thought this was about file sharing. Which of my files are safe to upload in a prompt, or publish in any media. That was not his point.

The original sin of the labs was training their models on the open internet without asking anyone. The courts have, surprisingly enough, mostly forgiven that sin. Training is fair use, as long as the material was obtained legally. The narrower crime, the training on pirated content, ended this summer in the largest copyright settlement ever written. Anthropic agreed to pay authors about three thousand dollars a work, a small fee to pay for the sin of the century.

Pamela Samuelson, who has shaped American copyright thinking for decades, sharpened her position. Copyright protects your wording, not the meaning of your content. You cannot get a model to recite a poem or chapter, but you can let it read every science journal and keep the knowledge. The law, she warns, guards the least valuable thing you publish.

Oh, and what about your own prompts and file uploads to LLMs? In which you might reveal a lot of information about strategy and business ambitions? Your enterprise contract already keeps those out of the training runs, so we can ignore that concern. Worth checking that your staff are not running company work through their private ChatGPT accounts.

Imagine you are a retailer that builds its Google search bidding on an agent running on Anthropic's models. No file that you upload can be accessed, or used for training. But the lab sees that this problem is worth solving, what a good answer looks like, and where its own model still falls short. Today that might be your competitive edge. And in two releases it is a feature your competitors can switch on. Satya Nadella described the mechanism: every time you use the tool and every time you correct it, the AI lab learns who you are. Your way of working comes back packaged in the next release, sold to everyone.

Figma, a leader in web design software, with revenue up nearly 50% in a year, lost more than three quarters of its IPO valuation. Anthropic shipped a capable free design tool, and the market concluded that what Figma does can be copied by a lab in no time. No files were stolen, all enterprise contracts were respected.

Karp's antidote to the exposure that is left: keep your ontology private, the map of what your data means and how it connects. Sound advice. Without that map AI labs cannot see what you are building.

But he is leaving much out. Something still has to run on top of that map, an orchestration layer that sees everything, and in Palantir's world that layer is designed and built by Palantir. Keep your ontology away from the labs, and hand the whole picture to Palantir instead. Remember how companies rushed into SAP in the nineties, then watched their best practices reappear in SAP's catalogue.

And, not surprisingly, there is a remedy he never mentions. Run models whose weights you can control. Join the open weight model ecosystem. Download them, tune them on your own machines, and nothing leaves at all. No contract to trust, no learning loop to feed. Chinese DeepSeek and Moonshot have shipped open models that land within a few points of the frontier at something like a seventieth of the price, free to run on your own servers.

Which is what makes Palantir's second alarm, a week later, even more suspicious. Days after praising American open models, its technology chief warned that China's open models are stolen American intelligence and ought to be locked down. The cure for value leaking to the labs has become a danger in its own right.

Not consistent at all, these two warnings. Unless you look at them from Palantir's point of view. The labs are moving into enterprise software, which is Palantir's own ground, so Karp attacks them for draining your value. Fear of China will drive defense budgets, so Karp's CTO Sankar attacks Chinese models, and the labs' sloppy protection of their weights.

Nobody yet knows which stack will win over time. And that uncertainty is what you should remember. You need to protect one thing: your ability to move. Hold your own ontology, keep the layer above it replaceable, keep the models underneath swappable. Take Karp's warning seriously. Just read it with his own interests subtracted, and keep your escape routes open.

Sources
Karp: enterprises are livid, the labs take your alpha
Alex Karp on CNBC · 1 July 2026

The alarm that opens the issue. On CNBC, Alex Karp accused the AI labs of draining value out of the enterprises that use them. His word for it was theft, and his examples were not about files: the labs, he argued, absorb the alpha, the way of working that makes a company win, through the very act of being used. The essay takes the warning seriously and then reads it with his interest subtracted, because Palantir sells the layer he recommends as the remedy. Watch the clip with both halves in mind. The mechanism he describes is real, and every version of the cure he offers happens to run through Palantir.

cnbc.com/2026/07/01/palantir-karp-open-ai-anthropic-tokens.html
Samuelson: copyright is a dead end for protecting your data
Pamela Samuelson on Lawfare's Scaling Laws podcast · July 2026

The legal ground under the essay's claim that the upload worry is settled. Pamela Samuelson, the Berkeley scholar who has shaped American copyright thinking for decades, walks through the AI copyright cases. Her core point: copyright protects the wording, and only the wording. Training counts largely as fair use when the material was obtained legally, the pirated-books cases end in settlements, and the meaning of what you publish, the knowledge itself, was never protected at all. A model can be barred from reciting your poem and still keep everything your poem taught it. For anyone hoping the law will guard their data position, she is the clearest voice explaining why it will not do that job.

lawfaremedia.org/article/scaling-laws--ai-copyright-lawsuits-with-pam-samuelson
Nadella: the moat is the learning loop, not the model
The Next Web · July 2026

Nadella supplies the mechanism behind Karp's anger. Even with training switched off by contract, the seller learns you as you use the tool: every prompt, every correction, every workflow shows the vendor which problem you are solving and what a good answer looks like. He calls it the reverse information paradox, the seller learning more about you than you learn about it, trace by trace. Coming from Microsoft's CEO the observation carries weight, since his company sits on more of those traces than anyone. It is the clearest statement of why protecting your data does not protect your position, which is the essay's central line.

thenextweb.com/news/nadella-reverse-information-paradox-ai-ip
Figma: value repriced overnight, no file stolen
The Motley Fool · 10 July 2026

The share price that proves the point. Figma, a healthy business with revenue up nearly half in a year, lost the bulk of its IPO valuation within months. No secret leaked and no contract was broken. What changed was belief: once Anthropic shipped a capable free design tool, the market concluded that what Figma does can be rebuilt by a lab in no time, and repriced the company accordingly. The Motley Fool piece walks through the numbers. The essay uses the case as the visible end of the mechanism Nadella describes: your edge can be copied out from above you, and the market does not wait for the copy to ship before it adjusts the price.

fool.com/investing/2026/07/10/why-figma-stock-lost-52-in-the-first-half-of-2026
Sankar: China's open models called stolen American IP
Shyam Sankar on Bloomberg · 15 July 2026

The second Palantir alarm, and the tell. Days after praising American open models, Palantir's technology chief warned on Bloomberg that China's open models amount to stolen American intelligence and ought to be locked down. Each warning makes sense read alone. Read together with Karp's, a pattern appears: the labs threaten Palantir's enterprise business, so the labs are the danger; fear of China lifts defense budgets, so China is the danger. The Chinese open models are today the most practical route to capable AI that feeds no American lab, and for Europe the shortest path to any sovereignty at all, which is exactly the route this warning talks down. The essay's advice: read the warning, subtract the interest.

DeepSeek V4-Flash: near the frontier, at a seventieth of the price
DeepSeek, model release · 31 July 2026

The remedy Karp does not mention, priced. DeepSeek's V4-Flash lands within a few points of the frontier models at something like a seventieth of the price, and the weights are open: download them, tune them on your own machines, and nothing leaves your walls. No contract to trust, no learning loop to feed. The essay's escape route runs through exactly this class of model, which is what makes Sankar's warning above so interesting to read against it. Whether an open model is good enough for your workload is an empirical question, and the benchmark linked here is the place to start checking.

Issue #1  ·  31 Jul 2026

A model that frames its own thoughts

The safe thing to say about a language model is that it only predicts the next word. Then Anthropic found a small workspace inside Claude where it holds concepts it never says, and showed that swapping one changes everything downstream. This essay takes the finding seriously, and then asks the harder question: how much of the richness is the model's, and how much is ours, projected onto it.

by Ebel Kemeling
Read this issue

On July 6th, Anthropic published a paper about the inner workings of Claude. To see why it caused a stir, it helps to recall how such a model works. A language model is layers of nodes, trained by tuning the connections between them until its predictions match the text it's shown. Once trained, it runs as a continuous stream: read what's been written, predict the next word, add it, repeat. There's no memory between conversations, and nothing we'd call a thought.

But the researchers found the model seems to hold concepts in mind that never appear in what it writes, stored in the 'J-space' (this is not a physical location, but a pattern spread across many nodes, identified with a mathematical tool called the Jacobian). When a concept is located there, those nodes light up far more than the rest.

An example: ask the model which currency is used in the country where the Eiffel Tower stands. To answer, it needs an intermediate step: the tower is in France, France uses the euro. So it tells you: euro, never mentioning France, since you didn't ask. Yet France is exactly what shows up in the J-space while the model works this out. Reach into the J-space and swap France for China, and the output changes accordingly.

Why is this special? Three things stand out: (1) the space is small, holding only a handful of concepts though nothing in the design demands that type of scarcity; (2) what's held there isn't being said, which is different from simply having a legible internal state; and (3), the special one: it is selective: some operations run through the space while others go around it. Together, that's more than most people expected a next-word predictor to do.

Neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, who has long argued consciousness is essentially a shared internal workspace becoming available to the rest of the mind, found this thrilling: maybe that's simply what any system needs to think flexibly, machine or brain.

For what the J-space seems to do, Linguists would use the word 'framing'. And how it does that, echoes George Lakoff's Don't Think of an Elephant, on how the few concepts we hold active decide what we can say. Told not to think about a concept, the model half-obeyed, the forbidden idea showing up in the J-space more strongly than if it had never been raised.

Lakoff goes much further than Dehaene. He believes that concepts are inherently embodied: a frame like 'cat' can't be separated from the bodily, sensory experience that gives it meaning. That sounds reasonable to most of us. Reading that Claude is "holding" the concept of a cat, we fill in everything the word means to us, warmth, weight in the lap, a whole cloud of sensation, and conclude something rich must be happening inside. There's no reason to believe that. For the model, cat is just a position in a web of words, close to purr and whiskers, far from carburetor. The richness is ours, projected onto Claude.

But. Strip the projection away, and what's left is still framing. That narrower version has real pedigree: a century ago, linguist Ferdinand de Saussure argued that words mean what they mean through their place among other words, not by pointing at things in the world. It is funny to see that this forgotten theory tells us exactly how meaning works in LLMs.

So the J-space is a step, and a real one. The model does more than we thought a next-word predictor would: it holds concepts apart from its own speech and lets them shape what follows. What it offers is a glimpse of how much can be done with words alone: a great deal more than we assumed, and a great deal less than we are tempted to imagine.

Sources
Anthropic: Concepts held, and not spoken
A global workspace in language models · July 2026

On July 6th Anthropic published a paper that drew a great deal of attention, which I guess was deserved. Claude turns out to hold concepts somewhere in its middle layers that shape what it goes on to say, while those concepts themselves are never said. That somewhere is not a real place. It is a pattern spread across many nodes, brought to the surface with a piece of mathematics called the Jacobian, hence: 'J-space'. The authors are bold in one direction and careful in another. They borrow the vocabulary of neuroscience: an opening section on conscious access, and five properties to distinguish the thoughts we can get at from processing we never notice. Claude, they find, has all five. But access consciousness is a functional notion, a matter of what is available for reasoning and report, and on the separate question of whether anything is experienced, they state plainly that they take no position. The philosophical implications, they write, are unclear and likely controversial. Yet, our take is that it does seem like a kind of breakthrough. Most unique is that the space is very small, with only a handful of concepts. Second, its contents are withheld rather than spoken. And third, it is selective, with some operations running through it and others going around. Together that is more than a next-word predictor was supposed to manage.

anthropic.com/research/global-workspace
Dehaene & Naccache: Access to the workspace is what we call consciousness
Does Claude possess a conscious global workspace? · July 2026

When Anthropic invited outside experts to comment, they went to the people whose theory they had borrowed. Stanislas Dehaene, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Collège de France, and Lionel Naccache, a neurologist at the Paris Brain Institute, built the global neuronal workspace model together with the neurobiologist Jean-Pierre Changeux. It is among the most influential accounts of consciousness in neuroscience, and among the most deflationary: no inner light, no additional ingredient, nothing a machine could not have. They are the finding's intellectual parents, and they respond accordingly. They call it a landmark, chiefly because nobody installed the workspace. It emerged. They also point out the limitations. Claude has no 'ignition', i.e. the sudden all-or-nothing threshold that marks conscious access in humans. No body. No episodic memory. No continuity of self. It is hard to imagine, they write, what it would be like to be conscious for the length of a single conversation, and then switch off. On qualia (a common concept in philosophy not about objective properties, but subjective experience) they are merciless. Push the intuition hard enough and you find a hidden dualism.

unicog.org
George Lakoff: A frame cannot be switched off
Don't Think of an Elephant! · 2004

Among the experiments in the Anthropic paper is one in which the researchers instruct Claude not to think about something, and then check whether it obeys. It half obeys. The forbidden concept shows up in the J-space less strongly than when the model is told to hold it in mind, and far more strongly than when nobody raised it at all. In another experiment the model is told a thought may have been planted in it, and asked what it detects. Its own first guess, which nobody suggested, is 'elephant'. Anyone with a background in philosophy or linguistics will then immediately think of a book by George Lakoff: 'Don't think of an elephant!'. George Lakoff, a cognitive linguist at Berkeley, broke with his teacher Noam Chomsky over whether syntax runs on its own, indifferent to what words mean. He argued that it cannot. Every word summons a frame, a structure of expectation, image and feeling, and no frame is cancelled by putting "not" in front of it. Nixon told the country he was not a crook, so the country saw a crook. For Lakoff, a frame reaches into the body: into metaphor, memory, the felt sense of a thing. Which raises a question he never had to answer, because in 2004 only humans could frame.

george-lakoff.com/writings
Zellig Harris: The method that became the machine
Distributional Structure · 1954

The oldest text here is the one that reads most like a description of current technology. In 1954 Zellig Harris, a linguist at the University of Pennsylvania, proposed that a language can be analyzed by tracking which words occur near which others, and that its structure will fall out of that distribution alone, with no appeal to what any word refers to. It was a proposal about method, written for linguists working with index cards. Seventy years later it is, in outline, how a language model is trained. The machine rests on a theory of meaning that its builders never needed to believe, or even to have read. The lineage is quarrelsome. Harris taught Noam Chomsky, who spent a career arguing that his teacher's method could never be enough. Lakoff then broke with Chomsky, and in doing so landed further from Harris than either of them: where Harris set the question of meaning aside, Lakoff put it back and put it in the body. The British linguist J.R. Firth said it best: you shall know a word by the company it keeps.

About

The Hedgehog & The Fox

We like to argue. About pretty much anything. And often we end up converging at a slightly higher level of understanding.

We both take an interest in AI, and we approach it from different angles. Martin from his expertise in analytics and big data, Ebel from the philosophy of language. Our daily lives give us exposure to how fast-growing digital native organizations adopt AI in practice.

We take inspiration from Isaiah Berlin's typology of the hedgehog and the fox. The hedgehog tries to understand by working through a problem. He does not diverge from his course, and progresses one step at a time. The fox approaches problems from the outside. Walks around it, trying different angles. Maybe one of us identifies a bit more as a hedgehog, and the other a bit more as a fox. But the point is that the fox and the hedgehog are strategies, not persons. We both use both of them.

In The Hedgehog & The Fox we bring our thinking on AI together. Each week we take one concept or one received opinion to task, guided by leading publications (so not the tweets of tech bros), and merge those ideas into a single essay. In that work, the I interests us more than the A. How must a complex system be organized to become intelligent, or more intelligent?

We do not claim to know where AI is heading, but we would gladly move the quality of the discussion forward. The least you may expect is to come away at a slightly higher level of confusion.

Martin & Ebel

Martin Heijnsbroek
I · The Hedgehog

Entrepreneur, board advisor in AI, and hard to stop once he starts calculating. Built Singapore Telecom's first customer database with his own hands, won McKinsey's global knowledge prize. Spent seventeen years advising boards on data strategies, well before AI became a boardroom word, and has two private equity exits under his belt. Taught Amsterdam UvA students for ten years how to drive impact from AI, wrote columns for the FD, while he built rewirenow.com as a leading AI services company.

Today he leads the Data & AI agenda of Sani Ikos Group, advises HomeDAO in Oxford and rewirenow.com, while he remains a crypto enthusiast, whatever the charts say. Can be more convincing than he is convinced, a dangerous trait for readers and friends. Only works with people he enjoys, is a big fan of Greece, and met Ebel at Insead auditorium, shooting at a simplistic bathtub metaphor.

Ebel Kemeling
II · The Fox

Entrepreneur, founder and board advisor in growth companies, particularly in energy transition and sustainability. Batteries, Solar, Synthetic fuels.

His fascination for AI started almost 50 years ago, when he first read Alan Turing's paper on thinking machines and accelerated when he met Heinz von Foerster two years later, which instilled a life long interest for complexity sciences.

Dubbed the cagefight philosopher by his professor in Philosophical Logic, he plays to win every argument. With logic, humor and facts, and if those don't work, confusion, deception and abuse.

He graduated during an AI summer, when neural nets and back propagation algorithms were hot. With AI, and particularly LLMs, it feels like the world is moving in a direction he thinks he can understand.

A jack of all trades, he is active as a board member of a flexible power platform (Return Energy), executive producer of film, author (The Opposite is also True) and owner of a beach club.

Read the TH&TF Manifesto: Turning the cards, on why we write this letter.

TH&TF Manifesto

Turning the cards

Artificial intelligence is not new. It goes back to the 1930s and the mathematics of computation. The war accelerated everything, and in the summer of 1956 the term Artificial Intelligence was coined. What followed became a seasonal rhythm. Extraordinary optimism, disillusionment, recovery. But since the early 1990s, the only way was up. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997. Deep learning remade computer vision in 2012. AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016. Huge breakthroughs, but not very visible to the public.

Enter ChatGPT in November 2022. Within two months, a hundred million people were using it. For the first time, AI was something anyone could use, every day. The technology had not suddenly changed. It had become visible. Plus, the richest people on earth placed enormous bets on it, the largest companies reorganized around it, and valuations reached gargantuan levels. Silicon Valley's marketing machine began pushing a story: this is the most important technology ever built, it will change everything, the only question is how fast.

That story frames how we privately speak about AI. But it is not always clear how. In our conversations, we use what cognitive scientists call chunks: ideas repeated so often they compress into a card you can play without checking what it refers to. "Hybrid systems always work better." "AI is ultimately a human matter." "Every job will disappear." "Machines cannot be creative." The cards get passed around and get nods of approval, without checking what it actually means, or if the person using the card has any idea what he is talking about.

These cards do not deal themselves. Nearly every card is dealt by a company that has an interest in you playing it. Anthropic says its models are too dangerous to share. OpenAI says it will drive the growth that pays for everything. Palantir warns against Chinese models. We are not clairvoyant, so we will not try to settle the matter. The best response is neither to believe them nor to dismiss them, but to take the arguments seriously, and understand them better than the people or companies using them.

Under all the cards hides the essence of the game we are playing: the understanding of what intelligence really is. Mostly we picture intelligence as a quality of a human brain. So the goal of AI, or even AGI, becomes to create an "Einstein in your pocket". But we also speak of smart teams, smart organizations, even smart cities and societies, and nobody thinks a city has a skull. So isn't intelligence a bit more than symbol manipulation inside a brain?

This is a platform for people who would rather think about AI than talk about it. The hedgehog and the fox, borrowed from Isaiah Berlin, are two strategies to approach a question. The hedgehog knows one big thing and follows it all the way down. The fox knows many things, circles around the question and keeps finding new angles. We use both, not to reach final answers, but to turn the cards over, one chunk, one thinker, one idea each week, and we try to uncover what it is about. You will be left not with conclusions, but hopefully will be a bit harder to sell to, and a bit better at asking the right questions.
